Southwell 'Roman villa' site saved from housing

Published

30 October 2015


Land thought to contain important archaeological remains has been saved from being used for housing after a mystery benefactor bought it for a seven-figure sum.

The site in Southwell, Nottinghamshire, is next to where remains of a Roman villa have previously been discovered.

The land has now been given to nearby Southwell Minster, which will act as custodian.

It can only be used for educational, conservation and cultural purposes.


The acting dean Canon Nigel Coates said: "It's a benefaction we never anticipated and he or she has been extraordinarily generous in giving us this site.

"It's their wish to remain anonymous but we do hope that in the future the connection with Southwell and the person's identity will be made known."

Southwell Minster already owned most of the land where remains of the villa have previously been found.

The development site used to belong to the minster too, but it was given to the Minster School, which built premises there in the 1960s.

The school later sold the land to raise money for new buildings in a different location, and the site became "an eyesore", external.


Newark and Sherwood District Council granted planning permission for nine houses, despite the plans being opposed by the Save Roman Southwell campaign.

Roger Merryweather, chairman of the Southwell Heritage Trust, said the benefaction was "absolutely amazing" for the town.

"We are extremely grateful to the benefactor for what he or she has done," he said.

"Now there will be the scope and the opportunity to recognise that area and perhaps preserve it better than it might have been preserved before."

Long-term plans have not been decided, but the site will be cleared of rubble, levelled and grassed as an immediate first step.


'Large and impressive' villa


The houses were due to be built on the former site of the Minster School, which has been demolished since the image above was created.

The original development proposal encroached on what is thought to have been the east wing of the villa, including the bathhouse. This area was removed from the development proposal following the discovery of a monumental wall.

Newark and Sherwood District Council said houses had not been permitted where the Roman villa was.

However, Dr Will Bowden, Associate Professor in Roman Archaeology at the University of Nottingham, said the villa complex would have extended onto the development site.

This is because excavation carried out on behalf of the developer revealed Roman remains across much of the site, including a line of Roman buildings.


"Villas were massive farm complexes with agricultural and industrial functions that could extend over a wide area," said Dr Bowden.

"As far as we can tell, it is one of the largest and most impressive villas in the region.

"It features extensive mosaic pavements and some very high quality wall painting, both located when parts of the villa were excavated in the 1950s."

The school was extended in 1971, and 225 bodies thought to be medieval were removed and reburied in an unknown location.

"They are a major lost archaeological resource," said Dr Bowden.

"It was partly this sense that the history of the town was being repeatedly eroded in this way that spurred the community protest about the development."

webpage.text:
Discovering Box Villa

Discovering Box Roman Villa   Research and photos courtesy Kate Carless  October 2020

John Hardy standing in room 5 amongst Sir Harold Brakspear’s excavations in 1903

The story of the excavations on the Roman Villa site is a long one. The site itself has been much disturbed as a medieval water-mill was built over it at the property now called The Wilderness and part of the west wing and the courtyard are still covered by the mill pond of that house. In fact, the medieval mill leat leading to the waterwheel cut through the pavements of two rooms (rooms 2 and 39). The pavements at the villa have been uncovered many times and left exposed to the weather before being recovered. Some of them have been wholly or partly destroyed by frost. 

Site of the excavated area of Box Roman Villa

Rev George Mullins’ Discovery, 1831
The first reported discovery was in 1831 by the Rev George Mullins, who owned The Wilderness at the time. An unknown author commented in The Gentleman’s Magazine of 1831 that previous parts of a tessellated pavement had been unearthed in a garden belonging to Mr Mullins, adjoining the churchyard but no spot could be pointed out where the same might with certainty be found.[1] In making some additions to a very old building, the workmen, on sinking for a foundation, struck upon the mutilated remains of a tessellated pavement about two or three feet below the surface of the ground. It appeared to have been part of a large square, and the part now discovered was evidently one of its corners. It had a wide ornamental border of no remarkable beauty.[2] The article mentions reports of other pavements in the area, it is said that several beautiful tessellated pavements had formerly been found in the churchyard and gardens adjoining. On the island in the ornamental fishpond of The Wilderness very many Roman tesserae of different colours and sizes were found.

Two years later Rev Mullins gave details of more finds on his land, seven stone pillars leading from the original pavement to another mosaic forty-three yards north from the pavement alluded to.[3] Near the stones was an altar-like erection, consisting of several stones, and a piece of stone of a semi-circular shape about a foot across and eight inches thick. He goes on to list more finds: a tessellated pavement of blue stone with two red borders, a wall on the south side with several flues and a regular hypocaust. At a depth of four feet below the surface of the earth, he discovered a third pavement, nearly perfect, apparently forming a passage from some part of the building. It is nine feet wide, twenty-eight feet long … it evidently extended much further in both directions. He talks about the wall plaster which he discovered being imitations of Egyptian marble, with elegant coloured borderings. This was the first reported evidence of the Box Roman Villa.

Victorian Owners of The Wilderness


There are periodic reports of finds in the area in the Victorian period. Harold Brakspear summarised these in his later article. In 1860 H Syer Cuming reported:
My garden is full of Roman remains—tiles somewhat ornamented, but broken, bricks, tessellated pavement, fused iron, &c. I send all away to mend the roads; they are a perfect nuisance. We cannot put a spade into the ground without bringing up these impediments to vegetable growth. There is a bath quite perfect, in the centre of the (Vicarage?) garden. It has been opened, but is covered up; and a beautiful pavement runs all about. The bits I dug up were white and black, very coarse work.[4]  Commenting on the discovery in 1892, the Rev EH Goddard was told that the finds came from a piece of ground adjoining The Wilderness.[5]

He went on to publish a report on the bath house wing with a   Harold Brakspear at the site
semi-circular, sunk space with a water course, the floor and
the sides of this well are covered with tesserae.[6] The
bath and the pavement had been removed and were for sale in
Bath and he led a visit to Box in 1895 to look at a small
patch of pavement which had been recently discovered
immediately opposite the north side of the church tower,
reporting that it is in a very disintegrated condition and
will probably not long survive exposure.[7]


Building Valens Terrace, 1900
John Hardy bought a plot of land just north of the vicarage
in 1897 to develop housing there (now called Valens Terrace
and part of the garden of the Wilderness). He quickly
uncovered more mosaic pavements and realising their
importance, re-covered them and began asking around for
professional archaeological help.

Hardy made a tracing of the Mosaics at Roman Villa. It was
much damaged by frost but the central portion, which
consisted of a two-ringed knot pattern in red, white and
blue, was lifted and framed and bought by Mr Falconer who
later gave a fragment of a piece from another room to the
Devizes Museum (no longer to be found there). To excavate
the site in 1902-03 John Hardy commissioned Sir Harold
Brakspear of Corsham, an eminent conservationist who had
worked on Bath Abbey, Windsor Castle and Lacock Manor.[8]
They uncovered a coin of the Roman Emperor Valens
(364-378AD) and named the rank of houses after him. The
wonderful photographs of the 1902-03 excavation were all
taken by Sir Harold’s brother.

Selwyn Hall Excavation, 1967-68
The last major excavation was in 1968-69 led by Dr Henry Hurst. The purpose was to establish a chronology for the main part of the site, and if possible, to fit into it the evidence from the previous season's work of a fourth century addition to the villa.[9]
Part of the north wing was re-examined and three main periods were distinguished: the courtyard in the first period; the second period involved the demolition much of the north wing, replaced by an apsidal-ended triclinium, 55 ft by 31 ft; and in the third period the triclinium was consolidated, its walls doubled and the external corridor replaced by two rooms. The report went on to say that the dating of the three periods is still far from certain.

The results of the excavation were published in 1987.[10] Evidence of a burnt layer of deposits was associated with copperworking remains and third and fourth-century pottery. The report confirms that Box had one of the richest collections of mosaic floors of any building in Roman Britain, with the remains of floors recorded in twenty of its rooms (equalling the total known for Woodchester).[11]

Box Roman Villa has never achieved the fame it deserves. This is partly because there is little evidence of it above-ground and no museum details apart from the model in the Box Library. It is also difficult to tell the full story of the villa as so much still remains to be discovered despite the efforts of the antiquarians and archaeologists mentioned in this article.

References
[1] Rev EH Goddard, Wiltshire Archaeological and Natural History Society, Vol XXVI, 1892, p.405-08
[2] Brakspear thought the work was in The Old Parsonage House which burnt down in 1853, being replaced by Box House - see Wiltshire Archaeological and Natural History Society, Vol XXXIII, 1904, p.236
[3] Reported by Rev EH Goddard in Wiltshire Archaeological and Natural History Society, Vol XXVI, 1892, p.405-08
[4] British Archaeological Journal 1860 (xvi, 340) reported by Harold Brakspear in Wiltshire Archaeological and Natural History Society, Vol XXXIII, p.238
[5] Rev EH Goddard, Wiltshire Archaeological and Natural History Society, Vol XXVI, 1892, p.405
[6]Wiltshire Archaeological and Natural History Society, Vol XXVI, p.405-08
[7] Wiltshire Archaeological and Natural History Society, Vol XXVIII, p.258-59
[8] Harold Brakspear, Wiltshire Archaeological and Natural History Society, Vol XXXIII, 1904, p.236-268
[9] Wiltshire Archaeological and Natural History Society, 1969
[10] HR Hurst, DL Dartnall and C Fisher, Excavations at Box Roman Villa 1967-68, Wiltshire Archaeological and Natural History Magazine, Vol.81, 1987, p.19-51
[11] HR Hurst, DL Dartnall and C Fisher, Excavations at Box Roman Villa 1967-68, Wiltshire Archaeological and Natural History Magazine, Vol.81, 1987, p.22

La première découverte signalée remonte à 1831 par le révérend George Mullins, propriétaire des lieux à l'époque, qui mit au jour un pavement en mosaïque tesselée en creusant pour des fondations, ainsi que d'autres vestiges tels que des piliers en pierre, un autel, un hypocauste et des enduits muraux imitant le marbre égyptien. Des fouilles ultérieures ont également été menées par Sir Harold Brakspear en 1903. Le site a subi des perturbations au fil du temps, notamment en raison de la construction d'un moulin à eau médiéval au-dessus.

Public Meeting on The Abbey Project, October 1

The Bury Society have invited its members and other local people to have their say on the Abbey of St Edmund, Reborn project at a public meeting on October 1st at The Guildhall, where the doors will open at 6.30.

This follows the consultation exhibition held in St Edmundsbury Cathedral from Friday 26 to Sunday 28 September.

Poster for Cathedral event

James Mellish summarises project

Alasdair Travers talks to patrons


The public meeting will be an opportunity to view panels explaining the proposals and to listen to a presentation about the project. There will then be time to ask further questions and to make views known. These views will be recorded as part of the public consultation.

The Abbey of St Edmund has a history stretching back more than one thousand years. Once one of the richest and most powerful Benedictine monasteries in medieval England, the story of the Abbey is central to the development of the town across five centuries. Made possible by National Lottery players, the Abbey of St Edmund, Reborn project will conserve and protect the Abbey ruins, build a visitor centre facing onto Angel Hill, expand and improve the footpaths around the site, and provide exciting interpretation and activities for all ages and interests.

The exhibition presents a series of 14 panels that outline the project’s emerging ideas, proposals and priorities, many of which have not been shared publicly before. Visitors will be able to find out how the Abbey’s extraordinary history is presented to visitors, plans for conservation and interpretation of the ruins, opportunities for education, community engagement, and tourism. Also, how the biodiversity of the site will benefit from the project and how new buildings may look.

Poster for Guildhall event

What is the project about?

Connecting the elements of the project


An illustrated half hour presentation from James Mellish (Project Manager) will explain details of the main elements of the project and how they all fit together.  This will be followed by questions and comments from the audience. This feedback will play a vital role in shaping the next stages of the project.

Martyn Taylor (Chair of the Bury St Edmunds Society CIO, a member of the Abbey Heritage Partnership) said, “The Bury Society offered to host this public meeting in addition to the public consultation exhibition, to give another opportunity to local  people to find out more details about this really important project for our town and how it might affect them. We care about Bury St Edmunds and it is vital that people have their say on what goes on here.”

The Bury St Edmunds Society CIO is a voice for local people to represent their views, especially with larger organisations. See www.burysociety.com for more information. It is a founder member of the Abbey of St Edmund Heritage Partnership.

The Abbey of St Edmund Heritage Partnership comprises over 20 organisations and individuals who care about the Abbey. St Edmundsbury Cathedral, West Suffolk Council and English Heritage (the Abbey of St Edmund, Reborn project partners) have come together as members of The Partnership to develop and deliver this project. Find out more at www.stedscathedral.org/abbey-st-edmund

Visiting Downside Abbey

Welcome


Downside Abbey is open to everyone, Monday to Friday 10 am to 4 pm throughout the year (excluding Bank Holidays)

You are welcome to visit whether you’re a pilgrim, tourist, visitor, or just passing by! 

Our guidebook is available to buy online before you visit (click here) or you can buy one from the abbey church when you’re here.   

Visiting Us

Coming from the A367 you will see signs to Downside Abbey, adjacent to our parish church of St Benedict’s, (roughly half way through the village). 

The entrance to the Abbey Church is at the end of the road (follow the red line on the map). There is designated parking for visitors in the green area; if this is full then please respectfully park adjacent to the abbey church, on the road. Keep walking towards the metal gates and the entrance will be to your left.

If you have any questions, please email us by clicking here.

If you are unable to make a physical trip to see Downside, why not make a virtual visit by clicking here.

Enjoy your visit!

n.b. please note that dogs are not allowed in the abbey church (except guide dogs). We ask you to kindly respect the dignity of this house of prayer which is a consecrated minor basilica and where the Blessed Sacrament is reserved. Mass is said on a Sunday at 10 am. All welcome.

family-history

Postcards from the Past 2026-125 – more kit – High Mediaeval merry widows

New Toy

Self indulgent, may be, but (I tell myself) practical. A camera body of the same type as mine so that I have a spare as I’m going on longer expeditions just to photograph stuff and it’s insurance against failure. Oh yes it is!

And a lens of just the right focal length range to fill the gap in my existing kit just happened to be in the display cabinet. It is no longer in the display cabinet.

So a camera body and a 45mm-200mm f4-f5.6 lens (90mm-400mm 35mm equivalent) now grace my take around kit. It’s not a fast lens, I don’t need speed, as in shooting for architectural purposes I use ISO 200 at f22, on a tripod as they are invariably long exposures. 

I now feel more confident as I’m not replying so much on a single point of potential failure.

And when I got home I entered it all on the database for insurance record purposes, and scared myself when I looked at the total.

Travel

All this meant that I had to go into the centre of Birmingham for the first time in nearly two years. It is no more pleasant than when I did that daily. I’m just glad that I live where I live.

Coming back, and because I had to combine the trip with shopping I decided that I’d pass by the old university site in Perry Barr, the first time in ten years that I’d done it in daylight, and was left wondering at the, shall we use estate agent speak, of the closeness and density of the flocks of bats (acknowledging the contribution of Reverend William Archibald Spooner (1844–1930) to the richness of the England language) they’ve built on the site. And the colour – a darkish muddy grey all over, surrounded by a building site.

These wrestlers supposed to be the accommodation for the 2022 Commonwealth Games, but were not completed in time – pandemic delays were blamed. They’re now affordable housing, I understand, or at least that was the original plan. The accommodation, the chaplaincy and other diverse buildings are no more. Flattened ground behind builders’ barriers seems to be the order of the day.

Powerful Women 

In research, because of the time going out, not much, save to say that of the powerful ladies of the high Mediaeval, two, who both happened to be founders of Cambridge colleges, Clare and Pembroke, were  close friends and associates who operated within the same high-ranking social and intellectual network in the fourteenth century. Marie de St Pol (Countess of Pembroke) was a frequent visitor to Elizabeth de Clare’s home, particularly at Usk Castle. Records indicate that Elizabeth entertained Marie regularly. They were both wealthy widows and influential patrons of art and education. Marie was likely inspired by Elizabeth, who founded Clare College, Cambridge in 1338, to establish Pembroke College, Cambridge in 1347. They maintained close contact until Elizabeth’s death in 1360. They shared a circle that included Queen Isabella (wife of Edward II). They were considered two of the most significant female figures of their time.

All of which leads me to the question – Elizabeth, Lady of Clare, likely financed some, at least, of the fourteenth century rebuild of St Peter’s, Bosworth. How important was that to her and how hands on was she? We know she held the advowson for the church, so that is an indication, but how closely she was physically involved is a question that needs to be studied, not that I expect and more detail to emerge.

It does form part of the story. Medieval merry widows springs to mind as a possible subject.

Spring?

During travel, heavy squally rain with quite a few lumpy white bits mixed in. Would someone please tell the weather that it’s May – in other words, late spring.

Postcards from the Past 2026-97 – St Anne proving elusive

Learnt about some more Saxon bones today – found n the current churchyard, which puts a whole new complexion on where St Anne and St Thomas was situated.

 1. St Peter’s Church
 2. Location of Makret Bosworth Chapel according to the record from  the Taxatio Ecclesiastica Database, a couple of hundred metres from St Peter’s (Taxatio, 2014)
 3. The locations from the Taxatio (ibid) are for St Peter’s SK407033 and for the Market Bosworth Chapel, which may be St Anne’s, SK408035
 4. Location of the nurses’ home which found Saxon graves when the foundations were excavated in the 1930s 
 5. Location of  St Anne’s Close (enclosed field) from the survey of 1592
 6. St Anne’s Hill, where Peter Foss places the original (Saxon) church, which may have been a chantry

Various questions and inconsistencies:

 1.  If we take the Taxatio location reference which was deduced from detective work by the database compilers, and the suggestion that ot was a chapel associated with the manor house, could it be a replacement for the original church on St Anne’s Hill?
 2.  The chantry existed until 1548 when it was suppressed.
 3.  If Sir Thomas Harcourt had a chantry chapel associated with the Manor House, why would he build another chantry as the south aisle of the Parish church a furlong away? They existed at the same time.
 4.  Is St Anne’s Close merely a field?
 5.  Quote from Nichols 1811, p501 “Ralph de Boseworth, deacon, was presented in 1223 to a chapel at Bosworth, sponsored by Richard de Harwecurt
 6.  An undocumented finding of more bones when the road from Carlton’s gradient was eased n the vicinity of St Anne’s hill to ease the passage of carts. When this happened I have yet to determine.
 7.  Was there a priory? Newman (1967) seems to think so.
 8.  For the school of 1094 (ibid) it was suggested that the original church has people, the priest and deacon, who taught.
 9.  One suggestion that the original as a Saxon Minster, but another that it was too small (with only priest and deacon) for it to be so.
 10. Just how many church sites can one small Leicestershire town sustain?

I really must get QGIS up and running so that I can map mediaeval finds to other information.

St Anne’s looks as if it’s going to be a fun rabbit hole,

And thanks to Charlotte and her two children (aged 11 and 9) for more feedback on the online guide.

On Linkedin I’ve been getting emails about apprenticeships in many fields open at Historic Royal Palaces (for which it tells me I’m not qualified, so why are they sending them?) at Hampton Court.

I can think of only one piece of music suitable.


Postcards from the Past 2026-48 – farmers’ market – migration of books

Th fourth Sunday of each month, except for December when it’s earlier, is the Farmers’ Market in Market Place. This was yesterday’s.

Today has been letter witting and cataloging and sorting books. There were teetering piles on the coffee table but the’ve successfully migrated to shelves and started to be grouped by subject. Some others have successfully migrated to a bag to be donated for loan, while some duplicated history subjects are going to migrate as reference to the Parish Office.

Temperatures are rising temporarily, so they say, and more photos are planned. I must also venture to Stoke Golding to compare rocks, so to speak, to see if the theory if the stones for the church are from Attleborough. Stoke Golding church is built from Attleborough stone, so matching is possible although not certain.

Wikipedia says this: “A now-disappeared local stone quarry was the source of “Attleborough Sandstone” a very popular high-quality building stone that was once used in the construction of numerous up-market buildings, particularly churches, in the local area. A noted example is the parish church, St Margaret’s, in Stoke Golding. The quarry operated from medieval times until the 1930s when the stone was worked out.”

Postcards from the Past 2026-18 – mills – water – wind – horse – hand

Part of the enquiry into the history of any place, but is seldom put into any prominence in written histories, must be “how did they feed themselves.?” We’ll start with mills to grind human and animal feed. This is long before the days of the potato being a source of starch, so grain was supremely important.

The 1086 Domesday Book records well over 5,600 to 6,000 watermills in England, and although Bosworth is in the upper 40% in Domesday, in terms of settlement size, no mill is recorded. They must have ground corn somewhere. Saxon remains have been found on Silk Hill as well as in other places but there is no mention of a mill. Other places are mentioned for location setting.

For mills we have to look at Nichols’ 1811 History of Leicestershire, where there is mention of mills powdered by water, wind, horse and hand in Bosworth, in various entries. Here I am quoting directly with translation or clarification in brackets and italics. I’ve left the Latin out.

In 1279, the following inquisition was returned Bosworth, Coton, and Karleton, are of the fee of Winton; and Richard de Harecourt holds in the same two carucates of land in demesne, and three parcs, and two mills, water and ventriculum (tr. stomach – literally). He also has in the same a market, and a toll-house, which they do not know by warrant. Likewise Richard has in villeinage in the same twenty-three acres of land, which twenty-five servants hold; and the said Richard has nine quarters. Likewise in freehold in Bosworth ten acres of land, which seven free tenants hold. Likewise. in freehold in Coton six acres of land, which four free tenants hold, and one quarter. Likewise in freehold in Karleton sixteen acres of land, which six free tenants hold. They also say that Theobald de Verdon has the advowson of the church. And it should be known that the said Richard holds the said tenements in scutage and service for half a knight’s fee, from the heirs of Winchester, and heirs of the king in chief. He has there a view of freehold and royal title, as fully as the heirs of Winchester. Of warren, chase, &c. nothing.

Notes

 * The mention of a market predates the charter granted by Edward III in 1285
 * In the Domesday Book, a carucate (from the Latin caruca, meaning “plough”) is a unit of land assessment used primarily in the Danelaw counties (north and east England) representing the amount of land that could be worked by a single plough team of eight oxen in one agricultural year. It is conceptually equivalent to the hide in other regions, generally measuring roughly 120 acres, though sizes varied based on soil quality.
 * The watermill sits on Carlton Brook which is a tributary of the River Sence, which flows between the villages of Carlton and Market Bosworth. It is possible that the mill has a Saxon origin but was not disclosed at the time of Domesday.
 * The Lord controlled the production of carbohydrate. However competition happened …

In 1294, it appeared that Thomas de Eshoe of Bosworth, and Robert le Moimer of Osberston, used to bring their corn to John de Harcourt’s mill, in the life-time of Richard de Harcourt, father of the said John, to the time of his death; but that then the said Thomas set up a hand-mill in his house at Bosworth, and the said Robert a horse-mill in his house at Osberston, and so withdrew the service which they owed to the mill of John de Harcourt aforesaid, to the disinheriting of the said John. 

In 1420, Thomas Harcourt, knt. was seised of the manor of Bosworth, with the view of frank pledge (tr. a system of joint suretyship common in England throughout the Early Middle Ages and High Middle Ages. The essential characteristic was the compulsory sharing of responsibility among persons connected in tithings), market, fairs, two mills, a common bakehouse, and with the suits and other profits and commodities belonging to the aforesaid mills and oven; and they were held of the lord of Beaumont 

The baking of bread was also controlled by the Lord of the Manor

In 1534, the Knights Hospitallers had 5s. a-year arising out of Bosworth mill, which had antienty (long ago) been part of the fee of Robert de Harcourt.

This is the only mention of the Hospitallers in Bosworth.

In 1783, in getting gravel seven feet from the surface of the earth, in a meadow near the mill there were found several large teeth, many of which were five or six inches long.

However Ice Age evidence comes back – what these teeth were is unknown. The most likely preservation is of something like a sabre tooth cat, and they were buried deep in the deposit, and sufficiently unusual to have been noted.

For food production, as part of the tie to the lord, peasants were often required to use the lord’s mill for a fee, while manual quern-stones were used for smaller, private tasks. However in the 1294 entry quoted above it seems that the hold of the lord could be challenged.

Home Farm, also mentioned, is a traditional British term for a farm that is part of a large country estate, typically located close to the main manor house. Historically, this farm was kept in the demesne (possession) of the Lord of the Manor, rather than being rented out to tenant farmers. It served as the primary source of food, produce, and fodder for the main household (the “home” or manor house), and was usually situated close to the principal residence of the landowner.

I have been thinking about what a friend said that getting schools involved, and I’m going to develop more of this type of story and see where it leads. Both the mill and Home Farm seem to be reasonable starting points.

More floor has appeared, temporally, at the expense of room on the sofa. I was juggling books and have come to the conclusion (which may be blindingly obvious to others) that an exit strategy for books is necessary. Hence there is a three foot high pile to go. I’m trying to find of local book exchanges and seeing if there’s any interest in some of Sandy’s sewing and quilting books and materials. I’d rather to go to someone who can use them rather than just be here for the sake of it. I have to dispense with the sentiment and look at the practicality.

Postcards from the Past 2025-74 – free-school – parsonage – maps and dates

I’m collecting and correlating evidence. What seems straightforward leads to more complexity and side tracks that are very interesting in themselves

One of the things in the Market Bosworth society archive is an annotated map of 1592, The area around the church interests me for a number of reasons, not the least because of dates. The map is dated 1592. I now refer to the buildings numbered 5, the free-school, and 6, the parsonage, on the key. Clicking on the map will enlarge it.

Source.

These are the query points, from Nichols: Source. Nicholls, J (1811), History and Antiquities of the County of Leicester, Volume 4, part 2. Link.

 * Building 5: In the year 1593 he begun the foundation of a free-school, built with ashler stone, for grammar scholars …
 * Building 6: The Rectorial House, seen on the left of the Church in Plate LXXVIII, is not the least in consequence among those of that order in the county. It was built by the Rev. John Dixie, who died in 1719.

I could think that the free school (building 5) which was started in 1593 replaced an earlier building, but I do not know of any documentary evidence for it, or it may be an assumption on the part of the map compiler.

Building 6 could not be the Rectorial House as described above, but could there have been a previous parsonage on the site?

This uncertainty means the the map illustrated cannot be taken as gospel.

And for my friend Robert, this is the evidence I was referring to about the position of the free school from our conversation about a week ago.

As a reminder these are the illustrations I’ve already used for the free school and the Rectorial House. The style of that building could not have existed in 1592.

From what I can tell the only building now present from this map is the church itself, although digging deeper, and the reason I’m looking at all listings on Historic England, is that the Red Lion, which is on the corner opposite 4, labelled Bayly, mentions a sixteenth century core. I must make a nuisance of myself by going round taking pix off listed buildings. 

Domestically, clearing, washing and sorting clothes to donate so that I can try to move around the building. There’s still a lot to do.

resultats_lens.texte_contexte: Récit personnel évoquant l'acquisition d'un nouveau boîtier d'appareil photo et d'un objectif pour des expéditions photographiques, combiné à un déplacement dans le centre de Birmingham et sur l'ancien site universitaire de Perry Barr, qui devait initialement servir de logement pour les Jeux du Commonwealth de 2022 avant d'être transformé en logements abordables en raison de retards liés à la pandémie. Le texte aborde également des recherches historiques sur de puissantes femmes du Moyen Âge, notamment Marie de St Pol (comtesse de Pembroke) et Elizabeth de Clare (fondatrice de Clare College à Cambridge), amies et mécènes influentes au XIVe siècle.
